The two issues that *were* the wiring slices, #745 and #746, were both closed on 2026-07-23 — so `rotation/mod.rs:22`'s "production resolver wiring is #745/#746" is now a dangling pointer to closed work.

**Uncovered delivery — 7 slices, no issues exist for any of them:**

1. Concrete `ScopeRootPublisher` / `ChildIndexResolver` / `SweepResolver` / `WriteWavePublisher` over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient` — only fakes today
2. Facade command arms — `Share`, `Downgrade`, `CreateInviteLink`, `AcceptShare`, `RotateNow` all fall through to `EngineError::Unimplemented` at `facade.rs:1901`
3. Sweep idle-cadence Scheduler job — `run_sweep` has exactly one caller in the crate (`grants/create.rs:281`)
4. Scope-exit trigger consumption — `ReplayReport::scope_exit_triggers` is populated at `sync/rebase.rs:133` and read by nothing
5. Write-revoke / downgrade trigger → `rotate_scope_write` (trigger table is 3 of 5)
6. Discovered-link-expiry trigger (the other missing one)
7. Invites — ephemeral-key blobs, bearer write-link flagging, claim→grant conversion, ledger expiry field; 100% greenfield, only doc-comment mentions

Slices 2, 5 and 6 depend on 1. Slice 7 is independent (grant creation is landed). Note this also means #772 and #754 are effectively blocked by uncovered work — their stated preconditions live in slices 5 and 3.

**Recommendation:** mint those 7 as sub-issues under #635 with native `blocked_by` edges before any rotation agent starts — otherwise the work has no unit of assignment and the 10 existing children keep reading like the remaining scope when they aren't. number of actionable issues. Measured 2026-08-04 against a cleared board (0 open PRs, 59 actionable

same interface into ONE PR rather than trying to parallelize them — this also conserves the
CodeRabbit quota (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]]). Reserve worktree isolation
for the batches that genuinely run concurrently.

**PR #1021 open as draft**, `+320/−429` across 44 files — a net deletion, which is the right shape for a cleanup sweep. `MERGEABLE`, CI running, CodeRabbit correctly skipped (draft).

All seven issues implemented. Three deviations from the brief worth your attention:

**#1003 was solved differently and better.** Instead of minting a new `SecretField` newtype, the four payloads now derive over `SecretBytes` — which already redacts `Debug` and, after #998 landed constant-time `PartialEq`, *is* the newtype. It also folded in `seal::body::Version`, a fifth instance the issue's own comment cited but didn't list. This changes the guidance I gave you for #1015: new invite payloads should derive over `SecretBytes`, not a `SecretField`.

**#1000's conformance decision went the way I'd hoped but for a sharper reason.** The return value was dropped, but the agent found the retry-convergence assertion was only exercising at-or-below-floor entries — so it would have passed against a `commit_floors` that did nothing at all. It made an entry actually advance and added a same-key-twice-in-one-batch case in both orders. The coverage is stronger than what was removed, not merely preserved.

**Review gates caught three real misses**, all folded back: the hottest call site (`resolve.rs`) was still discarding the record and re-verifying downstream; a *fourth* `hex_lower` copy existed in `crates/engine/src/hex.rs` with seven importers; and a redaction test only searched for the hex spelling, so a raw `[u8; 32]` field rendering in decimal would have passed it silently.

Checks run locally were green including the wasm32 leg and a `getrandom` audit.

**One decision for you.** A reviewer argued the crypto-touching parts — the `ct_eq` hoist to `subtle::ConstantTimeEq`, `SecretBytes` gaining constant-time equality, and the four payload redactions — deserve their own ~200-line PR rather than riding along with 1,578 lines of mechanical cleanup. My brief mandated a single PR so the agent kept it whole. That reviewer has a point: constant-time comparison changes are exactly what you want a focused crypto review on, and they're currently buried in a diff whose headline is "cleanup". Splitting costs one extra CodeRabbit cycle.

Want me to split #1021 into a crypto PR and a mechanical PR, or leave it whole and just make sure the crypto review is run against the full diff?

Also noting: the second commit used `--no-verify` because the worktree has no `node_modules`. It's Rust-only so nothing lint-staged covers, and signing stayed intact — but flagging since it means the local hook chain didn't run.

Follow-up on PR #1021. The reviewer point you flagged was accepted: we're splitting the crypto-touching work out so it gets a focused review instead of riding along with mechanical cleanup. Do the split in your existing worktree.

TARGET SHAPE — two stacked PRs:

**PR A (NEW, based on `main`)** — branch `refactor/998-constant-time-and-secret-redaction`, title `refactor: hoist constant-time compare and secret redaction into core` (no parentheses). Carries:
- #998 in full — BOTH halves. The `floor::*` routing half is only two call sites (`net/publish.rs`, `rotation/sweep.rs`), so keep the issue whole rather than splitting one issue across two PRs.
- #1001 — `IpnsRecord` `Drop` removal, with your "nothing secret reaches a record" tracing in the body.
- #1002 — `hex_lower` hoist, including the fourth copy you found in `crates/engine/src/hex.rs` and its seven importers. It isn't crypto per se, but it lives in `crates/core/src/suite/*` and keeping all `suite/` changes in one PR preserves clean file ownership.
- #1003 — the payloads deriving over `SecretBytes`, plus `seal::body::Version`. This genuinely depends on #998's constant-time `PartialEq`, which is why both must be in this PR.
Body: `Closes #998`, `Closes #1001`, `Closes #1002`, `Closes #1003`.

**PR #1021 (rebase onto PR A's branch)** — keep the branch and title. Carries only:
- #997 — `fanout_get_verify` returning `VerifiedRecord`, including the `resolve.rs` carry-through fix.
- #999 — dead `NotAuthenticated` / `expires_at`, the re-pointed `drain.rs` tests, and the `json_authed` helper.
- #1000 — the dropped return plus your strengthened conformance coverage.
Body: `Closes #997`, `Closes #999`, `Closes #1000`, `Closes #719`. Retarget its base to PR A's branch (`gh pr edit 1021 --base refactor/998-constant-time-and-secret-redaction`) and note in the body that it stacks on PR A.

Ordering rationale so you can sanity-check the cut: PR A is based on `main` so its review isn't gated behind mechanical work; #1021 stacks on it because both touch `crates/engine/src/gate/floor.rs` (#998's `sequence_floor` routing vs #1000's `commit_floors` return) and because #1021 closes #719, which should only close once the whole set has landed.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Both PRs stay **DRAFT**. Do not mark ready, do not request CodeRabbit.
- Each PR must independently compile and pass tests. Run the full check set on BOTH branches separately — `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo test --workspace`, and the wasm32 leg. A split that only works when both are applied is not a split. I expect this to be the fiddly part: #1003 depends on #998, and #997 touches `net/publish.rs` near where #998's floor routing lands.
- `cargo fmt --all` — never scope to `-p`.
- Do not share `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` between the two branches; a stale reused test binary will make both report identical passing counts.
- Preserve commit signing; never `--no-gpg-sign`. `--no-verify` is acceptable again for Rust-only commits given this worktree has no `node_modules`.
- No Claude/AI attribution in either body.
- `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN` on every gh call.

Carry your existing findings into the right body — the redaction-test decimal-spelling fix, the `SecretBytes` doc correction, and the restored `ct_eq` in the two accept tests all belong to PR A; the `resolve.rs` re-verify fix and the conformance-observable strengthening belong to #1021.

Re-run `/crypto-privacy-review` against PR A's diff alone once split — that focused pass is the entire point of doing this.

REPORT BACK: both PR numbers and URLs, confirmation that each branch independently passes the full check set with the actual commands and results, and anything that resisted a clean separation. If some hunk genuinely cannot be separated, say so and explain rather than forcing it.

content.text:
# /loop — schedule a recurring or self-paced prompt

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

Manage the CodeRabbit review queue for FSM1/cipher-box while the user is AFK. Each iteration: (1) check open PRs and their CI status; (2) determine whether a CR slot is free (1/hr org-wide, last burned ~2026-08-04T00:22Z on #1022); (3) flip the highest-priority DRAFT PR to ready-for-review ONLY if its CI is fully green and no review is in flight; (4) verify any completed CR run actually posted a review pass ("Actionable comments posted:" or a submitted review) rather than a walkthrough-only, and re-queue it if walkthrough-only. Priority order: #1022 (crypto, never got a real review pass) > PR-6 client seams when it opens > #1014 rotation resolvers when it opens > #1021 (mechanical, stacked on #1022, lowest risk). CodeRabbit wanted expiry enforced in `reseal_scope_root` and `accept_share`. Both halves turn out to be unworkable:

- **`accept_share` structurally cannot see `expires_at`.** The deadline lives on `GrantLedgerEntry` → `WriteBody`, sealed under `kdf::write_key(kdf::write_seed(...))`. `accept_share` receives only the commitment and grant blobs; `GrantSection.write_body` is an opaque `SignedSealed`, and a read grantee never gets `write_scope_seed`. It cannot read its own deadline before *or* after `open_grant_blob`. Relocating the field somewhere accept could read it would put per-grantee data in the public grant section and lose the "observer learns only blob count" property.
- **Pruning expired rows at reseal is actively worse.** `reseal_scope_root` holds only the writer pseudonym, not the owner identity signer, so it cannot re-sign the commitment. Drop the ledger row → `enforce_committed_ledger` fails at *every* resolver, so one expired invite renders the scope root unadoptable. Drop only the blob → `NoBlobAtTag`, which `grants::revocation` treats as the definitive revocation signal — handing a write-grantee a capability-destroying lever on the one field the owner doesn't sign. Reseal is the write-grantee-executed path, which is precisely why `enforce_committed_ledger` guards it.

Correct removal is owner-only via `revoke_read_grant`, which cuts the tag from commitment *and* ledger and owner-re-signs — that's the discovered-expiry trigger, #1020, already scoped to part 2. CodeRabbit is right that `entry_is_live` has no production caller yet; that's the tracked gap, not something publish or accept can close.

The agent also caught that **CodeRabbit's premise on the second Major was factually wrong** — `invitee()` mints from `SeededEntropy::new(7)`, a deterministic stream, so the two `EphemeralInvitee`s had byte-identical key material and the assertions were *not* passing on a recipient mismatch. It applied the fix anyway, since the test was leaning on seed determinism implicitly rather than binding what it claimed to.

**Net production-logic change from the whole review round: zero.** Tests and one doc block. Expiry enforcement is exactly as it was, and the documented limitation stays as accurate as before.

Parse the input below into `[interval] <prompt…>` and schedule it.

## Parsing (in priority order)

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.

Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)

**Bugs the process caught that would otherwise have shipped:**

- `reseal.rs` signed the write body's structure signature at the **write** epoch while the gate recomputes at the **read** epoch — the first production revocation would have signed a permanently unadoptable scope root.
- Two independent rule-8 encode/decode violations, one of them pre-existing on `main` (`writeScopeSeed` could be sealed into a read grant via `PreservedFields`).
- `cappedBody` accepted `NaN`/`Infinity` caps, so the resource limit that PR added was bypassable to unbounded.
- `crates/contract` silently dropped `timeout_ms`, so calls the engine bounded to `CONTROL_TIMEOUT_MS` ran to the 30-second client budget.

**Four decisions waiting on you:**

1. **`expiresAt` outside the owner-signed commitment** (#1015 part 2) — a write-grantee can strip a deadline or forge one onto a victim's row. Fixing it structurally contradicts `blueprint/engine.md`'s "Expiry is a ledger field".
2. **Sweep versus the floor gate** (#1025) — converging below-floor records is what the sweep is *for*, but `gate::floor::check` rejects exactly those. Needs a sanctioned exception or a different source of truth.

result.output:
===== #1025 body =====
## Why this is not wiring

`SweepResolver` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/sweep.rs`) is the last read-plane rotation seam without a production implementation. #1014 landed the other two — `ChildIndexResolver` and `ScopeRootPublisher` — as `crates/engine/src/net/rotation.rs::OwnerRotationNet`, and deliberately stopped short of this one, because it is blocked on a design question rather than on plumbing.

The sweep exists to converge scope roots whose **published record epoch is below their durable read-epoch floor** — that is the epoch-lag predicate in `sweep_pass`:

```rust
if target.current_read_epoch >= floor_epoch { /* already converged */ }
```

But `gate::floor::check` rejects exactly those records:

```rust
if epoch < epoch_floor {
    return Err(... RejectionReason::EpochBelowFloor { floor: epoch_floor, epoch });
}
```

So a resolver built the way `OwnerRotationNet::gated_root` is built cannot obtain its own work-list: every node the sweep exists to repair is a node the adoption gate refuses. The lag is real and reachable — `floor::cold_seed` seeds a descendant's read-epoch floor from an owner-vouched re-point `minReadEpoch`, so a device can hold a floor above records that have not yet been swept.

## The question to answer

What authenticates a below-floor record that the owner is repairing, given AGENTS.md rule 6 — every resolved record passes the adoption gate, and a gate failure is fail-closed, never staleness?

Simply skipping the floor stages is not acceptable: a forgery-window writer re-serving a pre-rotation section would have the sweep republish a revoked grant set at the floor epoch — a silent revocation hole. `RootAdopter::recover_own_scope_material` faces the same shape and explicitly re-imposes what stages 4/5 would have checked; the sweep needs an equivalent, decided rather than improvised.

Candidate directions, none chosen:

- a repair-role gate variant that keeps stages 1-3 and 6 and substitutes an owner-held committed set for the record's;
- re-sealing from owner-held state rather than from the lagging record at all;

===== #1026 body =====
## Why this is not wiring

`WriteWavePublisher` (`crates/engine/src/rotation/rotate_write.rs`) is the write-plane rotation's transport edge. #1014 landed the two read-plane seams over the real network plane and deliberately stopped short of this one: three of its five methods are plumbing, but `republish` cannot be implemented against the seam as it stands.

The record handed to the publisher carries only routing identity:

```rust
pub struct RepublishedNode {
    pub node_id: [u8; 16],
    pub new_name: IpnsName,
    pub write_epoch: u64,
    pub is_root: bool,
}
```

Authoring the record at `new_name` additionally needs the node's read body, the read key it seals under, and — for a byte-stable republish — the predecessor name and its carried envelope fields. The wave holds all of them (`WriteScopeNode.current_name`, the resolved subtree) and hands over none. Closing that is a seam-shape change to a landed rotation primitive plus its simulation tests, not a net-plane implementation, so it wants its own review.

## Scope

1. Decide the shape: widen `RepublishedNode` to carry the authoring material, or hand the publisher a resolved-node handle. Keep the resume contract intact — `is_republished` must stay answerable from published state alone, with no in-memory carry across a crash.
2. Land the concrete `WriteWavePublisher` over `RecordTransport` + `ApiClient`:
   - `register` / `retire` over `net::register` and `net::retire` — already bounded and idempotent, reuse rather than duplicate;
   - `is_republished` over the fan-out GET;
   - `republish` over `net::author` + `net::record_publish`, signing under `kdf::ipns_keypair(write_seed(freshWriteScopeSeed, node_id))`;
   - `publish_repoint` across the three channels — scope pointer, mailbox, old-root tombstone.
3. Root linger stays: `retire` must never include the old root name, and `root_retire_ready` is still stubbed `false` pending the migration-window constant.

## Gate

Resumed name waves via the write-plane history link and crash recovery from published records only, per #635 — plus register-first ordering enforced structurally, so a publish of an unregistered name is impossible rather than merely unlikely.

content.text:
**86% of them are already stale** — 317 of 365 references in `crates/` point at closed issues. #746 alone appears 15 times, #745 ten times, #685 thirteen. Only 48 refs across 12 issues are live.

So: no, they shouldn't be there. The pattern fails for a structural reason — a comment saying "tracked by #1025" makes a claim about *the tracker*, which changes independently of the code, so nothing in CI or review can ever catch it drifting. Tonight produced four of these in one module: #745/#746 went stale, #1014 went stale the moment it merged, #1025 was pointed at the wrong seam, and `sweep.rs` still claimed `ScopeRootPublisher` was faked after #1014 landed it.

What the comment *should* carry is the fact, not the ticket: "no production implementation; tests fake this" is verifiable from the code, and stays true until someone writes the impl — at which point the comment sits right next to the change that falsifies it. The binding-contract prose on those traits is the genuinely valuable part, and it doesn't rot at all.

The dependency should run one way: issues point at code, code doesn't point back. An issue that names a stale file path is a nuisance; code that names a stale issue is a lie a reader can't cheaply check.

I hadn't opened the PR yet, so I've rewritten it to drop the numbers rather than re-point them:
